entry.title: ACTUAL START
entry.content:
LITTLE UPDATE

Alright so the reason I haven’t really been updating this blog is that I lost my secondary laptop’s password and the directory containing all the blog information was there so yeah pretty tragic. I’m now going to be updating this somewhat regularly though (hopefully). I know I already changed this project a bunch, but I just keep digging deeper into the OSdev rabbit hole and now I’m getting completely drawn to the idea of a riscv64 microkernel and working towards a working OS with a simple shell. Also, this article will just be a short update.

The gist of it

The gist of this project is to make a very minimal riscv64 microkernel with OPENSBI in the M-Mode and the microkernel in the S-mode, and have all the user drivers and all that in the U-mode. The goal of this is obviously still to be privacy focused, so I will still be trying to add as many security features as possible. I won’t be using AI for code generation because I mean, this is for learning.

What I’ve done so far

Not much. So far, I have the basics of risc-v down and currently skimming through OSTEP along with the xv6 book. I have set up the qemu environment and is starting to get some basics done. I’m still very much in the planning stage though, but I know I’ll need to go on high gear for this one because as much as I want to take my sweet time, college apps are right around the corner for me so I’ll have to keep that in mind. Of course, the enrichment of my understanding of low levle stuff is still the most important, but uh yeah I guess I’ll have to lock in and do it faster now lmaoo. Oh and I’m also first planning to make it single process just to get a single process working and then I’ll set up a queue system for multiple processes and I can’t even beging to think on how I’m going to implement simultanious processes. Really makes you think how crazy modern OSes really do. I think the short-term goal is to get a single process to work, because that’ll mean setting up memory, threads, and having places to put the input and output. Bascially, I’m not so sure myself yet, but I think the short term goal of a single process working is really nice because that’ll mean getting the resource allocation part done. I don’t think the queue system afterwards would be too hard?? but I guess we’ll have to see. Not seeing that far ahead for now.

Homework for me

  1. Actually start planning more comprehensively for the project.
  2. Work more on the project
  3. Update the blog more

Something a little extra

I recently got the CRAZYY ASSS OPPORTUNITY to do a mentorship?university? program (I don’t know what to call it), but basically some people at terasic will support me through an FPGA board project involving a TPU (or so I’ve been told). When I complete that project, I might combine the two projects together and run my riscv kernel on it or something. I’m completely unsure about this just yet, but maybe this is a possibility? Whatever ends up happening, I’m still really excited for the opportunity (honestly) and will be locking in on it. Yk it’s really funny cuz I thought there wasn’t any software under assembly and in turn machine code, but learning about FPGAs and Verilog and other HDLs, it’s just kind of blowing my mind at the endless opportunities. I think there is a debate whether HDLs are actually programming or software, but I personally think so from my very limited set of knowledge since you’re still compiling but with it being more physical than ever.

entry.title: Astralogy
entry.content:
Astralogy - KalmarCTF

Astralogy - 216 Points
Pwn/Binary Exploitation
Current Date: 2/28/2026

Challenge Information:

No Hints

Thought process Walkthrough:

So after extracting the files, there are a couple of files.

challenge.iso hardening.patch run.sh

When running the run.sh, it brings me to a virtual machine with a hobby distro called astraOS. I have no idea what that is, so I’ll just search up some information.

There’s also one executable file called exploit, except ./exploit doesn’t work.

Before that, here is the text we get after we run run.sh:

-bash: cannot set terminal process group (31): Operation not permitted (EPERM)
-bash: no job control in this shell
astral@astral:~>

The main observations here being that the initial neofetch is being done as root. This makes me think that it MIGHT be a VM escape or kernel pwn. Now isn’t it just great. I can’t even do some basic ass ROP and I’m not even good at heap stuff. If I solve this, I’m genuinely gonna pop champagne. ok, I also notice it says that it cannot set terminal process group because the operation is not permitted. I googled it and terminal process groups are the ones that have control over the terminal. It says it failed meaning I have control over IO.

First thing I do is get some idea of the environment and which tools are available:

The ./exploit doesn’t work with execute format error.

For now, we exit the VM and check out the hardening.patch since that should be giving us a detailed review of what they did to harden the OS.

Main things here are:

wrmsr stands for write model specific register(wrmsr) and it writes some value to a register. The MSR_FMASK register is the syscall register which is the toggle for users to run CPU features. The hardening being done in this line is that the changed 0x200 to 0x600. In this case, the actual hexadecimal isn’t the key here, it’s the bits. These bits are CPU flags and it controls what the users can do. The binary for 0x200 is 0010 0000 0000. The 9th bit is flipped. That bit controls the interrupts on syscall, which prohibits users to interrupt while the kernel is still setting up the registers and everything. Because the whole thing here is that the user needs to syscall and use some CPU features and so the kernel needs to set up some stuf first and the 9th bit just prevents that from happening. By chaning the 0x200 to 0x600, it is changing the bits to 0110 0000 0000. Ok, so it’s also flipping the 10th bit, which as the comment suggests, is disabling DF or the Direction Flag. This only changes a String Instructions such as memcpy or memset. The direction flag changes the order it is being copied or just how the instruction is being carried out. Normally, it would go from front to back. The DF simiply chages that and does the instructions back to front. The end results are still the same and everything, but it’s hardened becaues nobody would know if your stuff is copying from front to back or the other way.

The next one here changes the above. The changes are in the - and +. Again, since it’s CPU, it’s just changing flags and whatnot. In the original one, only the 9th and 10th bit are set to 1. The comment above explains it well. Those two bits are:

Bit 9 SFXSR (Operating System Fast FXSAVE/FXRSTOR Support):
This bit is part of the two bits that make up SSE. The scond bit is the 10th bit which I will explain later on. This bit adds support for XMM0~XMM15 registers. Those registers are used for complex math such as for cryptography, graphics, or 3D rendering. Another common usage is when a process is being closed and the cpu must really quickly save the state and data it had on so that it can be opened later on in the same state. Basically, it just enables these registers for sum big math.

Bit 10 OSXMMEXCPT(Operating System XMM Unmasked Exception Support):
This is features for those XMM registers(0~15). This cpu flag is to ensure no problems when an error is made. Without this, if there was an errror happening in the cpu process, it’d just crash, but this flag gives the control back to the kernel and makes it able to shut it down safely. The whole thing is KIND OF in the name it being OS XMM register unamsked(not hidden error) support for exceptions.

Update

Alright so first a little update I kind of forgot to update this blog and it is currently the second day of the event. I should be updating the Kernel project soon. I also really need to start locking in on that.

Day 1

So for the first day, I arrived onto the event location, attended the openning ceremony, and then started visiting the booths. Some standout booths were the CSCS(volunteering), AIS3, and B-Sides Tokyo. For the CSCS, at least from what they said, they’re basically doing the things that I’m already doing like pushing for open technology like Signal, Linux, wireguard, and stuff like that. And their targets are just peoppe who would be less tech literate like the elderly and younger kids. It also aims to foster interest in cybersecurity and open technology as a whole. I added their Signal so I might be doing these volunteering things later on. Of course, I’ll try to update this blog about it. For AIS3, it just stood out to me because it’s the summer camp that didn’t accept me because I wasn’t a Taiwanese citizen. I completely get it since it’s a government-funded program but still man I wanted to go. It seems like such a cool opportunity. Anyways, the third one is B-Sides Tokyo because they had a mini CTF challenge to get their stickers.

I think more than any booths or talks, the thing that stood out to me the most HAS to be the sheer number of people who are just like me. It’s honestly kind of surreal seeing a room full of people with their terminals open on linux and everybody discussing about RCEs, shitting on Windows, and all deeply passionate about cybersecurity and open tech. This whole environment just makes me feel completely at home. Not really related, but everybody is so shamelessly themselves in a good way. A good example of this would be the people’s anime wallpapers lmao.

In the afternoon, I went to listen to these talks:

  • UnPwn2Own Berlin 2026 / $70,000 Agent2Shell: Pre-Prompt RCEs in Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini
  • Vulnerabilities Assembled! The Vulnerability Factory Inside the Windows Kernel
  • Keychained Melody - Grabbing the Keys to the iCloud Kingdom
  • Harmonizing AI Agents and Human Analysts in CTI - Are CTI Agents Friends or Rivals to Junior Analyst

These were all really interesting, but I couldn’t take any notes because all my devices were out of juice and I forgot to bring my power banks.
Even though I didn’t fully understand a lot of these talks, I think that the most interesting ones were definitely the Pre-Prompt RCEs in Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini. I will be linking the conference talk notes at the end of this article)
These were all really interesting, but I couldn’t take any notes because all my devices were out of juice and I forgot to bring my power banks.
Even though I didn’t fully understand a lot of these talks, I think that the most interesting ones were definitely the Pre-Prompt RCEs in Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini(I will be linking the conference talk notes at the end of this article). What I found interesting was the general direction Mr. Tsuji chose to go. When people talk about AI security or AI CVEs, people usually think about prompt injection and trying to find exploits within the LLM. Instead, Mr. Tsuji chose to look in a larger scale and tried to find vulnerabilities from the AI agent’s permissions. Even though it is absoltely NOT a simple process, I was still surprised that these companies developing these AI agents didn’t catch onto these. The main issues are that these agents ask for permissions once and then the whole process gets root access basically forever. This is why those one or double click RCEs are possible. I think this problem ties into a bigger problem of people giving too much trust into AI.

Even though Mr. Tsuji’s talk was the most interesting for me, the talk that is actually most relevant to me would actually be the one on Harmonizing AI Agents. This is because in the talk, he pointed out the glaring issue in the whole software industry right now which is of AI replacing junior roles leading to the lack of senior talent in the future. The reason it is relevant to me is because I plan to go into the cybersecurity industry and the way companies are being recommended to use AI are very important. His talk also details how people should be using AI to learn about cybersecurity, so that part is also relevant for me as it shows how to improve at a faster pace.

entry.title: Motivation and Rough Planning
entry.content:
Initial Remarks

Even though this is a bit off topic, this is pretty much my first actual post on this blog. I know the KalmarCTF one was before this but I made that thing a while ago so this is my first post made FOR this blog. It’s also the first project I’ll be fully documenting on this blog. Also, sorry if this post isn’t very structured. I’m still new to writing these blog posts. I’m sure I’ll get better at it as I make more posts.

Motivations

Alright guys, so I’ve known about LFS(Linux From Scratch) and BLFS(Beyong LFS) for quite a bit and since I’m also planning this summer to configure and move to Gentoo as my daily drive on my main laptop, I was just like hmmmmm, what if I also just made a fun LFS build just to learn a bit more about how linux works. Later on, I realized that I could make it a bit polished with BLFS and swaywm to it and rice it a little to make it a full hobby distro.

After brainstorming it a bit, I thought that it would be cool that since I’m interested in cybersecurity and specifically pwn and rev, to just make a minimal linux distro with some tools and stuff already made. I’m sure somebody else has already done this type of stuff, but it’s really just for my understanding of linux and also to have some fun with it.

That is literally the entire reason why I’m doing this lmaoooo💀💀. Maybe I’ll think of some more grand reason later on when I finish the distro and make a page for it.

Rough Plan

I already finished making the html pages for LFS and BLFS(holy shit it is long). As you can tell from the top, this post is made on May 24 and I really only plan on actually following the LFS and stuff in the Summer. I also got exams as well, so I’ll only be able to actually do stuff once school ends. From now till then, I’ll just try to read over the LFS to get a good idea of what it is doing.

Later, I’ll configure the LFS first by following the guide. As of now, I still don’t know jack about how it’s going to go so I can’t really say any specific thing but I’ll just follow the LFS to get a base CLI distro then I’ll follow the BLFS to get a swaywm thing on top. I honestly can NOT bother with GNOME or KDE stuff. I have a feeling that the apps and dependencies that come with those would kill me before I make a full distro.

After the initial configuration, I’ll make that into an iso to understand how that process works.

Then, I’ll go back and this time, I’ll diverge from the main LFS guide and install OPENRC as my init. Probably with some help from some AI and random geniuses in Discord groups I’m in.

Vision

So the vision is to obviously have a minimal distro with a minimal riced swaymd and a bunch of security features in the distro turned on. The init system will be OPENRC in the end and it’ll also come with some pwn and rev tools such as gef or ghidra or binary ninja.

Final Stuff

I really have no idea how big of a project I’m getting myself into but I’m pretty exicted to get started. Yuuhhhhh, in these projects, I’ll also try to give myself some listed homework at the bottom to just keep myself on track.

Homework

  • Skim through LFS and BLFS guide to get a rough idea
